title: How To Stem The Tide Of Student Questions
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the problem of unchecked student questions derailing lesson pace, arguing that questions are valuable but must be controlled in both timing and topic. His central recommendation is to open designated 'question segments' tied to specific topics rather than allowing an all-day free-for-all. He advises never taking questions during instructions, offering post-it notes so students can jot down questions to ask later, and setting aside a couple of daily moments for open-ended questions unrelated to the lesson. The piece also recommends refusing to answer repeated questions or respond to call-outs, hand-waving, or students approaching out of turn, instead enforcing a consequence. Linsin frames the approach as a balance between encouraging curiosity and protecting instructional momentum.
points: Restrict questions to defined 'segments' tied to a specific topic rather than allowing them all day long.
Never take questions while giving instructions—wait until you're finished.
Give students post-its to jot down questions so they can let go of them until question time arrives.
Refuse to answer repeated questions or call-outs; redirect students to ask a neighbor or enforce a consequence.
Set aside two or three short 'ask me anything' windows a day so curiosity has an outlet without derailing lessons.
quotes: The most important key to managing questions is to tightly control when they may be asked. If you allow an all-day question free-for-all, which is surprisingly common, your progress through the curriculum will be a frustrating plod.
It’s best to allow for questions only during specified segments throughout the day. So at any given moment the floor will either be open to questions or it won’t.
Never answer a repeated question. It encourages students to tune you out. Instead, ask the student to check with a neighbor as soon as independent work begins.
Call on students who are sitting with their hand raised in the manner in which you modeled. Don’t respond to those who approach you, wave at you, or call out to you . Instead, enforce a consequence.

It’s important your students feel encouraged and motivated to ask questions and participate in their learning. But at the same time you’ve got to keep the pace of your classroom crisp and moving forward.
